description: Food choices linked to seven named religions, ethical beliefs, food intolerances, and common allergies.
content_html:
Food, Faith, Ethics and Health

What a person eats is often deeply connected to who they are — their faith, their values and their body. Understanding these connections is essential for anyone cooking for others. A school canteen, a hospital kitchen and a catering company all need to be able to prepare food that respects religious requirements, accommodates ethical choices and avoids allergens or intolerances. This lesson covers all seven religions named in the specification, the key ethical factors, and the medical distinctions between intolerances and allergies.

Religious and Cultural Food Choices

Religion shapes food choice through rules about which foods are permitted, which are forbidden, how animals must be killed, and how food is prepared. The seven religions you need to know are Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Rastafarianism and Sikhism.

Buddhism: Most Buddhist traditions emphasise compassion for living beings. Many Buddhists are vegetarian, avoiding meat and fish entirely. Some stricter practitioners also avoid onions, garlic and other pungent vegetables. However, there is diversity — in some East Asian and Tibetan traditions, consuming meat is permitted.

Christianity: Christianity has few universal food restrictions, but specific denominations and seasons introduce rules. Catholics and some Anglicans traditionally abstain from meat on Fridays and during Lent; fish is eaten instead. Seventh-day Adventists often follow a vegetarian diet. Food plays a central role in Christian celebration — Easter, Christmas and harvest festivals all involve specific traditional foods.

Hinduism: Many Hindus are vegetarian because the cow is considered sacred and harming animals conflicts with the principle of ahimsa (non-violence). Beef is avoided by virtually all Hindus regardless of other dietary choices. Some devout Hindus also avoid pork. Dairy products (milk, ghee, paneer) are commonly consumed and used in cooking. Fasting on specific holy days is common, and certain foods may be avoided on those days.

Islam: Muslims follow halal dietary law. Pork and all pork products are strictly forbidden (haram). Alcohol is also forbidden, which means it cannot be used in cooking — wine-based sauces are not suitable. Animals must be slaughtered by a Muslim who says a blessing at the time of killing, and blood must be fully drained. Shellfish is considered makruh (discouraged) in some traditions but permissible in others.

Judaism: Jews who observe kosher dietary law follow kashrut. Pork and shellfish are forbidden. Permitted animals (e.g. cattle, sheep, chicken) must be slaughtered in a specific way by a trained butcher (shochet). Crucially, meat and dairy must never be mixed — a Kosher kitchen has separate utensils, pots and surfaces for each. This means a creamy chicken pasta or a beef lasagne with cheese topping is not Kosher.

Rastafarianism: Many Rastafari follow Ital food principles — foods should be natural, unprocessed and ideally organic. Pork is strictly avoided. Many Rastafari are vegan or vegetarian. Alcohol and stimulants are typically avoided. Salt and chemical additives are also often rejected, so meals are seasoned with fresh herbs and spices rather than processed seasonings.

Sikhism: Sikhs who follow the Khalsa code avoid beef (out of respect for Hindu heritage in the Punjabi region) and halal or kosher-slaughtered meat — both methods involve prayers during slaughter, which is seen as objectionable. Many Sikhs are therefore vegetarian. Those who do eat meat choose the jhatka method, where the animal is killed instantly without a religious blessing. In Sikh langar (community kitchen), food served to all is always vegetarian so it is inclusive of everyone.

Key Fact

Summary of key restrictions: Pork forbidden — Islam, Judaism, Rastafarianism, Sikhism. Beef avoided — Hinduism, Sikhism. Meat and dairy not mixed — Judaism (Kosher). Often vegetarian/vegan — Buddhism, Hinduism, Rastafarianism, Sikhism. Alcohol forbidden in cooking — Islam, Rastafarianism.

Ethical and Moral Beliefs

Many people make food choices based on values rather than religion. The five ethical areas in the specification are: animal welfare, Fairtrade, local produce, organic food, and Genetically Modified (GM) foods.

Animal welfare: Consumers who are concerned about how animals are treated choose free-range eggs, outdoor-reared pork or certified welfare-label chicken over intensively farmed alternatives. Some avoid meat altogether on ethical grounds.

Fairtrade: The Fairtrade mark guarantees that farmers and workers in developing countries receive a fair price for crops such as coffee, chocolate, tea and bananas. Choosing Fairtrade products reflects a concern for global economic justice.

Local produce and organic food: Buying locally produced food reduces food miles and supports regional farmers. Organic food is grown without synthetic pesticides, herbicides or artificial fertilisers. Both choices involve paying a premium for ethical or environmental reasons.

Genetically Modified (GM) foods: Some consumers avoid GM foods due to concerns about long-term health effects, environmental impact (e.g. herbicide-resistant superweeds) or corporate control of the food supply. Others accept them as a valid technology for increasing yields. Current UK labelling rules require GM ingredients to be declared on packaging.

Students frequently confuse intolerance and allergy. An intolerance is a non-immune digestive reaction — the body cannot properly process a substance. Symptoms are usually uncomfortable but not life-threatening (bloating, diarrhoea, stomach pain). Examples: gluten intolerance (the protein in wheat, barley and rye causing digestive distress) and lactose intolerance (inability to digest the milk sugar lactose, causing gas and bloating). An allergy is an immune-system reaction that can be severe and potentially life-threatening (anaphylaxis). The body recognises a harmless protein as a threat and mounts a rapid, systemic response. Nut allergy is the most commonly tested example — even a trace can trigger anaphylaxis. The six named allergens you need to know are: nuts, egg, milk, wheat, fish and shellfish.

Food Intolerances

Gluten intolerance ranges from mild sensitivity to coeliac disease, an autoimmune condition in which gluten triggers an immune response that damages the lining of the small intestine. People with coeliac disease must avoid all wheat, barley and rye. Recipe modifications include using rice flour, buckwheat, maize flour, gluten-free oats or certified gluten-free pasta. Lactose intolerance means the body cannot digest lactose because it lacks sufficient lactase enzyme. Symptoms include bloating and diarrhoea after eating dairy. Modifications include using lactose-free milk, plant milks (oat, soya, almond) and lactose-free cheese or yoghurt alternatives.

Key Fact

The six named allergens you must know are: nuts, egg, milk, wheat, fish and shellfish. These are legally required to be declared on pre-packed food labels in bold text. A reaction to any of these can be severe; nut and shellfish allergies in particular can cause anaphylaxis, which is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate treatment.

You need to be able to select, modify and make recipes for different groups. Practical examples: a chicken casserole can be made halal by sourcing halal-certified chicken and replacing white wine with chicken stock. A pasta bake can be made gluten-free by substituting gluten-free pasta and flour for the sauce. A birthday cake can be made suitable for a lactose-intolerant guest by using plant-based spread and oat milk. A spaghetti bolognese can be adapted for a vegetarian by replacing beef mince with Quorn, soya mince or a mixture of mushrooms and lentils. Justifying your choice means explaining why each modification meets the dietary requirement, not just naming the substitute.
exam_tip_html: Questions on religion and food choice often ask you to describe or explain the dietary rules of a named religion. A common mistake is giving only one point per religion. A 3-mark Describe answer needs three distinct pieces of information — for example, for Islam: pork is forbidden (1); alcohol cannot be used in cooking (1); animals must be slaughtered by a Muslim who says a blessing and blood must be fully drained (1). On 6-mark extended-response questions about adapting a recipe for a specific dietary group, make sure you explain why each modification is needed, not just what it is. “I would use rice flour because rice is naturally gluten-free, which means the dish is safe for someone with coeliac disease” is a developed point; “I would use rice flour” alone is not.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Seven religions with specific food rules are named in the specification: Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Rastafarianism and Sikhism — know the key restrictions for each.
  • An intolerance (e.g. gluten, lactose) is a digestive issue that is uncomfortable but not usually life-threatening; an allergy (nuts, egg, milk, wheat, fish, shellfish) involves the immune system and can be fatal.
  • Recipe modifications must be justified: explain why the substitute ingredient meets the specific dietary requirement of the named person or group.

practice_questions.text: Name the food principle followed by Muslims that governs how animals are slaughtered and which foods are permitted.
State two food restrictions followed by observant Jews when keeping a Kosher diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two valid points: pork and pork products are forbidden; shellfish are forbidden; meat and dairy must not be eaten together / must be prepared on separate surfaces with separate utensils; animals must be slaughtered by a trained shochet using the correct method. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a food intolerance and a food allergy, using one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: food intolerance is a non-immune digestive reaction causing uncomfortable but usually non-life-threatening symptoms (1); a food allergy is an immune-system reaction that can be life-threatening (anaphylaxis) (1); valid example of intolerance such as lactose intolerance causing bloating (1) or valid example of allergy such as nut allergy causing anaphylaxis (1). Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Sanjay is preparing a birthday dinner for his Hindu grandparents who are strict vegetarians and do not eat beef or pork. He wants to serve a spaghetti bolognese. Explain two modifications he should make to the recipe, giving a reason for each change.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per modification (2 required). Modification 1: replace beef mince with a plant-based alternative such as lentils, Quorn, soya mince or mushrooms (1); because beef is avoided by most Hindus as the cow is considered sacred, and plant-based proteins are suitable for vegetarians (1). Modification 2: check the pasta does not contain egg (some fresh pasta does) or use a certified egg-free dried pasta (1); because some strict vegetarians also avoid eggs depending on their interpretation (1). Other valid modifications accepted: replace any meat stock with vegetable stock; ensure any cheese used is vegetarian rennet; justify clearly each time.

practice_questions.text: A school is planning a whole-school celebration lunch that must be suitable for students of all religious and cultural backgrounds represented in the school, including Muslims, Jews, Hindus and Rastafari. Explain how the caterer could plan the menu to meet these requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): clearly explains why each religious group's requirements affect specific dishes; identifies overlapping restrictions (e.g. no pork satisfies multiple groups; a fully vegetarian menu using plant proteins satisfies all); explains specific substitutions with reasons (e.g. halal-certified meat satisfies Muslim students; plant-based dishes with Ital-style fresh herbs satisfy Rastafari principles; no meat-and-dairy combinations in the same dish respects Kosher principles; vegetarian options satisfy Hindu and many Buddhist students); considers label transparency and allergen marking. Two or three well-developed reasoning chains using accurate vocabulary.

Secure (3–4): addresses most religious groups with some development; mostly accurate; some application to the practical catering scenario.

Developing (1–2): names some restrictions with little explanation or development; limited application to menu planning.

Emerging (0): superficial points only; no religious requirements correctly identified.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how ethical and moral beliefs such as animal welfare, Fairtrade and views on GM foods can influence food purchasing decisions, using examples throughout your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): breaks ethical food choice into distinct components; animal welfare (1) — link between intensive farming and low price vs welfare certification and premium cost; consumer may pay more for free-range eggs or outdoor-reared pork because they value reduced animal suffering, which means demand for cheap intensively farmed products falls among ethically motivated consumers (2). Fairtrade — farmers in developing countries receive guaranteed floor price; consumer choice to buy Fairtrade coffee funds community development but typically costs more; analyses the trade-off between personal cost and global justice (2). GM foods — opposition linked to uncertainty about long-term health effects or environmental concern (superweeds, monoculture risk); support linked to yield increases that reduce food prices or can address food insecurity; analyses both sides (2). Examines how these beliefs interact with income (ethical choices often more expensive; affluent consumers more able to act on values). Accurate vocabulary throughout.

Secure (5–7): addresses at least two ethical areas with reasonable development and some analysis of relationships and consequences.

Developing (2–4): describes ethical factors with limited analysis; one-sided or descriptive.

Emerging (1): lists terms with no development.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes the Kosher rule about meat and dairy?
options: Meat and dairy can be eaten in the same meal but not cooked together
Dairy is forbidden entirely for observant Jews
Meat and dairy must never be mixed; separate utensils and surfaces are used for each
Only beef and dairy cannot be combined; chicken and dairy is permitted

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a food intolerance (not an allergy)?
options: Lactose intolerance causing bloating and digestive discomfort
Wheat allergy causing a severe immune response

knowledge_checks.q: The food philosophy of many Rastafari, emphasising natural and unprocessed plant-based foods, is called _____.
A certification scheme that guarantees producers in developing countries receive a fair price for crops such as coffee and chocolate is called _____ trade.
Match each religion to its key food restriction.
right: Pork is forbidden; animals must be slaughtered following specific rules
Beef is avoided as the cow is considered sacred
Meat and dairy must never be combined; pork and shellfish are forbidden

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'halal' mean in Islamic dietary law?
flashcard_questions.a: Permissible; food prepared in accordance with Islamic law, including specific slaughter rules.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'kosher' mean in Jewish dietary practice?
flashcard_questions.a: Meeting the requirements of Jewish dietary law, including separation of meat and dairy.

flashcard_questions.q: What food does Islam strictly forbid?
flashcard_questions.a: Pork and all pork products; also alcohol including in cooking.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key Kosher rule regarding meat and dairy?
flashcard_questions.a: Meat and dairy must never be mixed; separate utensils and surfaces are required.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do most Hindus avoid beef?
flashcard_questions.a: The cow is considered sacred; harming it conflicts with the principle of non-violence (ahimsa).

flashcard_questions.q: What is Ital food in Rastafarianism?
flashcard_questions.a: Natural, unprocessed plant-based food; pork and alcohol are avoided.

flashcard_questions.q: What food is served in a Sikh langar (community kitchen), and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Always vegetarian, so it is inclusive of all regardless of dietary restrictions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a food intolerance and a food allergy?
flashcard_questions.a: Intolerance is a digestive issue (uncomfortable, not life-threatening); allergy is an immune reaction that can cause anaphylaxis.
Difficulty digesting the protein gluten (in wheat, barley and rye), causing bloating and digestive pain.
Inability to digest lactose (milk sugar) due to insufficient lactase enzyme, causing bloating and diarrhoea.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six allergens specified in this course.
flashcard_questions.a: Nuts, egg, milk, wheat, fish, shellfish.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Fairtrade mark guarantee?
flashcard_questions.a: Producers in developing countries receive a fair price; extra funds go to community development.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one reason why a consumer might avoid GM foods.
flashcard_questions.a: Concern about long-term health effects, environmental impact, or corporate control of food supply.

glossary_terms.definition: Arabic for 'permissible'; food that is prepared and sourced in accordance with Islamic law, including specific rules for animal slaughter.
Food that meets the requirements of Jewish dietary law (kashrut), including rules about permitted animals, slaughter methods, and the separation of meat and dairy.
The Rastafari food philosophy, centred on natural, unprocessed plant-based foods and the avoidance of meat, salt, additives and alcohol.
A certification scheme that guarantees producers in developing countries receive a fair price for their goods, with additional funds for community development.
Difficulty digesting the protein gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye, causing gastrointestinal symptoms such as bloating and abdominal pain.
The inability to digest lactose, the natural sugar in milk and dairy products, due to insufficient production of the enzyme lactase.
